RagShortTexts: Inquisitorial testimony is recorded through an institution with coercive authority.
Denunciation, penance and imprisonment affect households as well as accused individuals.

Variants.Content: Papal bulls entrusted inquisitorial authority to the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, who were already famed for their learning and discipline. Traveling inquisitors carried portable archives, and they recorded secret denunciations in cross-referenced parchment registers that could be checked against each other years later. Those convicted of Cathar or Waldensian heresy faced forfeiture of their estates, perpetual confinement, or secular execution when they relapsed after penance. The inquisitors saw the procedure as the only way to root out a faith that hid among neighbours and kin. Local lords were expected to cooperate or face excommunication. The registers they compiled became a lasting record of heresy and of the communities that lived under suspicion.

An inquisitorial record is made through questions, testimony and a notary's choice of words. A scholar must read it as evidence produced by a coercive institution, not as a transparent transcript of village belief. Penance and reconciliation are possible outcomes, alongside imprisonment and referral to secular power; procedure does not erase the danger of denunciation.

When investigators summon witnesses, an old quarrel can acquire a frightening new importance. A household wants to know who has spoken, what was recorded and whether a relative may return. Fear can silence neighbours as easily as produce testimony. Neither a whispered accusation nor a notary's neat writing proves that every charge against the village is true.
